title: The History of Sugar. Why Sugar Killed More People Than Any War in History
fullText: Picture the perfect industrial facility. A rigid split between unskilled labor and highly trained specialists. Three ships running 24 hours a day with no holidays and no breaks. A strict linear layout where raw material flows from one mechanical station to the next with almost zero wasted time. Total standardization of the final product and a workforce at the machines that's completely endlessly interchangeable. Sounds like a cotton mill in 19th century Manchester, right? Wrong. This is happening nowhere near Ford's assembly lines or those [music] Manchester weaving sheds. So, where are we? 17th century Jamaica. This is the boiling house of a typical Caribbean plantation. That comforting sweetness in your morning coffee has a history that starts far, far away from any quiet farm field. Sugar was history's first truly merciless industrial machine. This human processing apparatus was running at [music] full capacity centuries before Europe's first coal furnace ever lit up. On the surface, it looked idyllic. The classic oil painting scene. Endless green fields, windmill blades turning lazily on the horizon. But underneath that picture postcard exterior sat something closer to a strict industrial system. Europeans of the time were used to a gentle agricultural rhythm. Grow your wheat. Bring in the harvest. Store it in a dry barn. Take it to the mill whenever it suited you. Sugar cane destroyed that peasant logic completely. A cut canetock starts rotting and fermenting within 24 hours. The juice spoils almost instantly. The plant's biology set a brutal deadline. From the swing of the machete in the field to crystallized molasses, you're counting hours, not days. Either the cane gets processed immediately or the entire harvest is lost. There was no such thing as a cane warehouse. That desperate race against time gave birth to an entirely new kind of economy. The technology arrived on Barbados from Dutch Brazil around 1642 and the island transformed almost overnight. Small farms collapsed one after another. Wealthy land owners bought up the land and stitched it into massive agroindustrial estates. A typical estate covered roughly 500 acres. 200 of those were dedicated entirely to one non-stop crop. Over a single 15-month cycle, a plantation like this could produce 600,000 lb of sugar. Even the cheapest grade musado brought in around 7 12,000 lb sterling. Greed demanded more. So the owners started experimenting. Investors tried shrinking the growth cycle from 15 months down to 12 to speed up returns. Yields collapsed. So how do you make up for a harvest that just cratered because you rushed it to avoid losing a single precious minute in transport. Buildings on Barbados were built in cascading tears from the start. The mill sat on the highest ground. Crushed cane juice ran downhill by gravity through stone or wooden gutters straight into the boiling house. The mill itself was a massive rig with several cylindrical rollers. Workers fed stiff cane stocks in by hand to squeeze out every last drop. The stocks got run through twice. That doubled the physical strain on the workers and stretched out every processing cycle. Historical records treat it as routine when an exhausted worker got dragged into the rollers. Ledgers and chronicles from the period casually log these mangling accidents right alongside the day sugar output. During harvest season, the workday stretched to 18, sometimes 20 hours. Overseers organized brutally precise labor gangs with tightly scheduled shifts. After a full day in the fields, workers were pulled into an additional night shift at the boiling house. Processing continued by torch light. Every minute of the day was regimented down to the shift and the schedule. The beating heart of this operation was the boiling house. Archaeological records and archives from the University of Glasgow paint a picture of the single most dangerous spot on the entire estate. Juice from the mill dropped into a holding tank, then flowed into a clarifier where it was heated. From there, the scalding liquid was ladled down a chain of copper and brass kettles, each one smaller than the last. The liquid boiled continuously, slowly reducing down into thick syrup. The heat near those furnaces was extreme. Open vats splashing droplets of boiling molasses, floors that were perpetually wet and slick. Enslaved boilermen balanced heavy ladles against a punishing schedule. Deaths from burns and heat stroke were a regular occurrence. A rigid hierarchy ran through this work, too. A skilled boiler was worth far more on the market than an ordinary field hand. His trained eye, knowing exactly when to pull the boiling kettle off the heat, determined how much usable sugar came out at the end. That kind of expertise made certain workers extremely valuable property. The human cost this machine consumed is staggering. Jamaica's own records tell the story in cold numbers. Between 1748 and 1788, the island imported more than 335,000 enslaved Africans. 40 years later, a census counted just over 226,000 people still alive. The machine was chewing through human beings faster than ships could bring in replacements. Even after that grueling endless [music] shift, there was no rest. Workers were sent off to tiny plots of land to grow their own food. Why would plantation owners spend money feeding people when the workforce could just farm their own scraps of land after a full shift? Spatial control, clockdriven labor, and an unbroken production line all fused into one system. Sugarcane built an algorithm where a human being was purely a consumable input for maximizing profit. The boiling houses of Jamaica and Barbados were only the end points of a much larger global network. To grasp the true scale of it, look at the ocean routes through the eyes of a ship owner in Bristol or not. A merchant's worst nightmare in any era is an empty cargo hold. Loading a gallion in the Caribbean with molasses and sugar bound for the home country was only half the job. That ship had to sail back to the islands, too. If it crossed the Atlantic empty, that wasted return voyage would eat up a massive chunk of the profits. Out of that problem came what history would later call the golden triangle. In modern logistics, arbitrageing demand gaps between regions without ever touching your home port is considered elite level strategy. In the 18th [music] century, mercantileist Europe was already running exactly that playbook. On the first leg, heavy cargo ships sailed from European docks toward the coast of West Africa. Holds packed with manufactured goods, metal ingots, copper cookware, factory-made textiles, and crates of musketss by the hundreds at fortified coastal trading posts. That cargo of weapons and cloth was traded directly for enslaved people, purchased from local traders for the middle passage across the ocean to the Americas. The decks were radically reconfigured, turned into multi-level shelving with less than a meter of clearance between tiers. Captains started circulating printed diagrams built specifically to calculate every inch of deck space for maximum loading. On arrival in American ports, the survivors were sold at auction. The proceeds were immediately converted into colonial export crops. The now empty decks were refitted again, packed with barrels of sugar, tobacco, and bales of cotton, and the ship set course for home. France or England. Every leg of the voyage paid for the next one. Fresh profit got generated every single time the anchor was raised. The mercantalist economy ran flawlessly. Colonies supplied cheap raw materials to the mother country and served as a captive market for its finished goods. The state skimmed a steady stream of profit off customs duties. [music] Sugar functioned as hard currency, the thing that pulled three continents into one shared trade ledger. Inside this cycle, human beings were fully reclassified as depreciating equipment. Surviving plantation account books show a chillingly practical approach to death. By some estimates, an enslaved African on a Caribbean cane plantation had an average life expectancy of about 7 years. Plantation owners treated that mortality rate as a straightforward math-based cost of doing business. Given the cost difference, it was simply cheaper for plantation owners to keep buying fresh adults off incoming ships than to invest in keeping already exhausted workers alive. turning hundreds of thousands of people into standardized tradable capital demanded sophisticated tools for protecting that investment. Transatlantic voyages were long and dangerous. Storms, disease, the works. Keeping the triangle trade running smoothly required serious financing and a way to spread out the risk. These voyages weren't only funded by big merchant magnates either. Lawyers, doctors, and property brokers in port cities all bought shares in these expeditions, chasing dividends from colonial cargo sales. It was precisely the need to service these supply chains that fueled the rise of the maritime insurance industry, the same institutions that would go on to build the financial power of the city of London. The surviving insurance contracts from that era are written entirely in the cold language of shipping manifests. Phrases like share of cargo, loss in transit, extent of compensation, language engineered to hide the brutal reality underneath. The absolute low point of this legal fiction was the case of the British ship Zong in 1781. The ship was crossing the middle passage. A serious navigational error by the captain badly delayed the voyage and drinking water ran critically short. Facing the prospect of losing the entire cargo, the crew made a chilling calculated decision. Over the course of several days, they threw 132 people overboard. What happened next is the truly shocking part. [snorts] Once the ship returned, its investors filed a direct claim with London insurers demanding compensation for lost property. The legal battle that followed was fought entirely over the wording of a commercial insurance policy. British maritime insurance rules of the time were crystal clear on this point. Losses from jettisoning cargo to save a ship were fully covered. But if enslaved people died in the hold from thirst or dysentery, that was filed under natural spoilage of goods, and insurers paid absolutely nothing for that. From a pure cost standpoint, the captain's decision was mathematically rational. What else could the captain do when death by thirst meant zero payout for the shareholders, while throwing people overboard guaranteed a full payout? For months, courts debated those 132 stolen lives as a routine precedent on the limits of property damage. The economic system had learned how to translate human existence into debits and credits, ensuring death itself successfully. Nothing could stop the triangle trade through appeals to compassion. Because credit had already welded European stock exchanges, African trading posts, and Caribbean plantations into one self-perpetuating machine. And this machine didn't just finance individual ships. It held entire nations hostage. Wars themselves became first and foremost tools for protecting investments. In 1763, negotiators sit down in Paris. The 7 years war is over. France has lost and under the peace terms must give up part of its overseas territories. Two possessions are on the table. On one side, New France, modern-day Canada, millions of square kilometers of forests, lakes, and fur trapping grounds, an area half the size of Europe. On the other, Guadaloop, a tiny volcanic speck in the Caribbean that colonial officials could ride across on horseback in a single day. Britain offers France the choice of which one to keep. and France's foreign minister, the Duke Desoiselle, hands over the entire northern continent to Britain just to hold on to that tiny island. From today's vantage point, that looks like one of the great blunders of history. But customs ledgers from the 1750s tell a very different story. Canada's total annual exports of timber and beaver pelts brought the French treasury about 14,000 pounds sterling a year. Guadaloop in that same period produced roughly 600,000 lb worth of sugar. That one small island was out producing every single British Caribbean colony combined. Voltater writing at the time mocked the two empires for tearing each other apart over what he called a few acres of snow. Snow doesn't feed factories and it doesn't pay off loans. London was caught in its own version of this madness. The victorious British crown voluntarily handed back its most profitable prize. A tightly organized block of MPs, merchants, and plantation owners, the so-called West India interest, sat in parliament. They owned land in Jamaica and were terrified of internal competition. If Britain had annexed Guadaloop with its enormous output, cheap French sugar would have flooded the London market. That would have crashed prices and wiped out old fortunes overnight. So the plantation lobby leaned hard on the cabinet, arguing that continental security mattered more than grabbing new tropical territory. In 1759, a British fleet stormed Guadaloop. The British took control of its boiling houses and sent home glowing reports claiming the island's plantations alone could cover half the crown's war expenses. Four years later, London politicians simply handed it back. British strategists had convinced themselves that taking Canada from France would permanently secure their North American colonies from any northern threat. Lining up customs records against the map of military campaigns reveals an unsettling pattern. Empires weren't bargaining over square [music] miles. They were bargaining over tonnage. Future wars would be measured in barrels of rum. By keeping Guadaloop and neighboring Martineique, France held on to access to the 18th century's version of sweet oil. That resource funded armies and kept credit flowing. Britain, meanwhile, got an endless northern continent that demanded garrisons, forts, and staggering amounts of infrastructure spending. That perfectly rational logic had one fatal side effect. The moment the threat of French invasion from Canada [music] disappeared, American colonists no longer felt they needed London's soldiers protecting them. With the external enemy gone, the colonies suddenly started asking why they were paying taxes to a distant crown at all. One historical reading of events holds that removing the French threat knocked out the very thing keeping the colonist loyal and helped set the stage for the American Revolution. While European capitals redrrew [music] borders on paper, the machine kept spinning in the Caribbean. An island powerful enough to outweigh half of North America at the negotiating table remained a zone of total human burnout. Death rates on Guadaloop's cane fields consistently topped 10% a year. The population was sustained purely by a constant resupply of people from Africa. British abolitionists would later write bitterly that the empire had traded black lives for snow in the colonies and then washed its hands of the whole thing. Global politics was chained to a narrow strip of tropical climate. Controlling that climate zone became in the eyes of empires the key to global dominance. And that assumption held perfectly right up until the early 19th century when the whole system got blindsided by two completely unforeseen forces. The ambitions of a Corsican artillery officer and a dusty patent from a Prussian chemist. In 1806, Napoleon signed the Berlin decree [music] launching the Continental Blockade, an economic chokeold aimed at Britain. Napoleon wanted to seal off every European port to English goods and cut London off from its markets. Britain's navy answered in kind, clamping down its own naval blockade on the continent. Trade routes across the Atlantic ground to a halt. Warehouses emptied out fast. Continental Europe lost access to cane sugar entirely. The answer to that problem had been sitting in a dusty academic archive for decades. Long before the Napoleonic Wars, a German chemist named Andreas Sigisman Margraph ran a series of experiments at the Berlin Academy of Sciences and proved scientifically that ordinary beets contained crystallizable sucrose. Later his student Fron Carl Ashard refined the extraction process. A small processing plant opened up in Prussian Seleia. In peace time that chemical breakthrough [music] went nowhere commercially. European beets had too little sugar content and production costs were skyhigh. As long as Barbados and Jamaica kept shipping cheap molasses across the [music] ocean without interruption, there was no financial reason to bother with an inefficient beet factory. German authorities simply ignored the discovery. The blockade forced [music] everyone to redo the math. Cut off from ocean trade, Napoleon looked at that forgotten patent and saw a strategic resource. He ordered large-scale government-backed experiments to scale up the technology. France rolled out subsidies for beet growers, the first program of its kind in history, a government bonus specifically for an agricultural sector. A decree set aside enormous tracks of land for planting the new crop. By some estimates, around a 100,000 hectares were converted to sugarbeat. Meanwhile, French researchers Benjamin Delesay and Jean Baptiste Carowell took a shard's process and overhauled it completely. They dramatically boosted sucrossse yields, finally making the extraction commercially viable. The state poured money [music] into building imperialcale factories and opened specialized technical schools [music] to train workers. Within a few years, an entire industrial infrastructure had sprung up around beet sugar. On January 1st, 1813, Napoleon officially banned the import of all colonial sugar into France. The Continental blockade was designed as a military weapon, but it accidentally triggered an agricultural revolution. The Caribbean's climate monopoly collapsed. Dependence on the tropics simply vanished. There was no longer any need to send massive fleets across [music] the ocean or fight wars over scraps of island territory. The market share numbers over the following decades tell the story of that once invincible sugarce empire collapsing in slow motion. By the early 1850s, beet sugar accounted for [music] roughly 14% of global production. By the start of the 20th century, that figure had climbed to about 65%. The historic tipping point came in 1883 when global beet sugar production overtook cane sugar for the first time ever. The Caribbean's economic engine started falling apart. On top of Europe's technological breakthrough, came a demographic shift in the colonies. The abolition of slavery, including France's 1848 decree, cut off the plantation owner's free labor supply. Manual cane labor suddenly became expensive. Competition from European beet sugar combined with brutal labor disputes made the whole trade too risky to bother with. Massive fortunes simply evaporated. Once priceless islands turned into economic ruins, St. Croy, once one of the great hubs of the old sugar trade, slid slowly into decline. The last major plantations there shut down in the late 1920s. The final harvest at the island's Bethlehem sugar factory happened in 1966. After that, production there stopped completely. Sugar lost its status as a luxury good for good. In northern Italy, a glut of cheap sugar fueled the explosive growth of the mass confectionary industry. In Turin, producers started blending scarce cocoa with the now cheap local sugar and hazelnuts. Who could have guessed that mixture would become the foundation of a global chocolate spread industry? The industry crossed the ocean fast. In late 19th century Alvarado, California, the first profitable American beet processing plant opened its doors and the new industry took root across the American West. By the midentth century, growing beets had become routine work for countless small farms in Weld County, Colorado. Sugar had officially become junk. The exact same white powder that once redrew the map of the world in the 18th century now sells by the bag at any discount store. The old sugar producing centers lost their economic power and the planters lost their fortunes. It looks on the surface like a happy ending. Technological progress defeating colonial madness. Sugar faded into the background. But the machine it built 400 years ago never actually stopped. It just shed its biological skin. The formula perfected in those boiling houses turned out to be universal. Stop the presses and you lose raw material that rots within a day. In that system, a human being loses all individuality. He becomes an interchangeable part with a calculated shelf life measured down to the month. The Caribbean Islands became history's first testing ground for global supply chains. Capital and market sat in the city of London. The factory floor sat in the tropics. Cheap labor got shipped in from a third continent. In the humidity of the boiling house, humanity perfected the immortal machinery of the modern multinational corporation. The scale of this experiment is still staggering today. Researchers estimate that somewhere between 12 and 20 million people were shipped to the Western Hemisphere. Around 20% died just crossing [music] the Atlantic on the Middle Passage. Nearly 40% of the survivors ended up specifically in the Caribbean. The French in the 18th century openly called the Antilles the sugar islands, land that existed purely to grow one insanely profitable crop. Local food farming was wiped out to make room for it. And because local farming was completely wiped out in favor of monoculture, the islands themselves ended up on the brink of famine, permanently dependent on imported food. The model turned out to be almost too effective. It survived both the abolition of slavery and every technological shift that followed. A sweat shop economy where the real cost of a product is hidden behind the poverty of workers on the other side of the world scaled up to run the entire global economy. Other raw material industries copied the plantation playbook wholesale from cotton farming to oil drilling. Every time you order fast fashion sneakers or buy a smartphone assembled on a massive Asian factory floor, you're using an infrastructure built for cheapening human labor. Its founding principles were written in blood on Barbados. Once the outright buying and selling of people was formally banned, plantation owners simply switched to debt bondage contracts and started mass importing workers from Asia instead. That was the early prototype of today's offshore labor system. Even in the raw material sector, that colonial era division of labor never really disappeared. This centuries old sugarce framework is still standing strong. In 2016, the world grew almost 2 billion [music] tons of sugar cane compared to 277 million tons of sugar beat. And while Kane once again dominates by raw volume thanks to new producing nations, Europe's old dependency and colonial monopoly are gone for good. Today's biggest raw sugar producers are Brazil, India, and China. The processed refined product now comes mostly from temperate nations, Russia, France, the United States. The tropics still supply the raw green tonnage. The wealthy nations process it and control the money that flows [music] through it. The echoes of those old colonial fortunes are baked directly into the foundation of the industrial world. After all, wasn't it Caribbean sugar money that helped finance Europe's railroads and its very first factories? The system has burrowed deep into the human body itself. The average European eats about 37 kg of sugar a year. In Russia, that number climbs closer to 40 kg. The average American consumes roughly 190 g a day. Back in the 13th century, England's King Henry III could barely get his hands on three lbs of sugar for a [music] royal banquet. It was that rare, that precious a spice. Today, it's an invisible filler in almost everything [music] we eat. Sugar may well be history's first mass market fully legal addictive commodity. One that fused a physical dependency with an entire culture built around craving something

Cây mía đã phá hủy hoàn toàn logic nông dân đó. Thân cây đã cắt sẽ bắt đầu thối rữa và lên men trong vòng 24 giờ. Nước trái cây gần như hư hỏng ngay lập tức. Cây mía sẽ được xử lý ngay lập tức hoặc toàn bộ vụ thu hoạch bị mất. Không có cái gọi là kho mía. Cuộc chạy đua tuyệt vọng với thời gian đó đã sinh ra một loại hình kinh tế hoàn toàn mới. Công nghệ này đến Barbados từ Brazil thuộc Hà Lan vào khoảng năm 1642 và hòn đảo này đã biến đổi gần như qua đêm. Các trang trại nhỏ lần lượt sụp đổ. Các chủ sở hữu đất giàu có đã mua đất và biến nó thành các khu công nghiệp nông nghiệp khổng lồ. Một khu đất điển hình có diện tích khoảng 500 mẫu Anh. 200 trong số đó được dành hoàn toàn cho một vụ mùa không ngừng nghỉ. Vì vậy, các chủ sở hữu bắt đầu thử nghiệm. Các nhà đầu tư cố gắng thu hẹp chu kỳ tăng trưởng từ 15 tháng xuống còn 12 tháng để tăng tốc trở lại. Sản lượng sụp đổ. Theo một số ước tính, một nô lệ châu Phi trên một đồn điền trồng mía ở Caribe có mức trung bình tuổi thọ khoảng 7 năm. Các chủ đồn điền coi tỷ lệ tử vong đó như một chi phí kinh doanh đơn giản dựa trên toán học. Những chuyến đi xuyên Đại Tây Dương rất dài và nguy hiểm. Bão tố, dịch bệnh, công trình. Chính nhu cầu phục vụ các chuỗi cung ứng này đã thúc đẩy sự gia tăng của ngành bảo hiểm hàng hải, các tổ chức tương tự sẽ tiếp tục xây dựng sức mạnh tài chính của thành phố London. Những hợp đồng bảo hiểm còn sót lại từ thời đó được viết hoàn toàn bằng ngôn ngữ lạnh lùng của bản kê khai vận chuyển. Các cụm từ như chia sẻ hàng hóa, tổn thất trong quá trình vận chuyển, mức độ bồi thường, ngôn ngữ được thiết kế theo giấu đi sự thật phũ phàng bên dưới. Điểm thấp tuyệt đối của tiểu thuyết pháp lý này là trường hợp của người Anh tàu Zong năm 1781. Con tàu đang băng qua lối đi giữa. Lỗi dẫn đường nghiêm trọng của thuyền trưởng khiến hành trình bị trì hoãn nặng nề và nước uống chạy rất ngắn. Trước nguy cơ mất toàn bộ hàng hóa, thủy thủ đoàn đã tính toán ớn lạnh phán quyết. Trong vài ngày, họ đã ném 132 người xuống biển. Điều xảy ra tiếp theo mới thực sự là phần gây sốc. Tổn thất từ ​​việc vứt bỏ hàng hóa để cứu một con tàu đã được bù đắp đầy đủ. Từ quan điểm chi phí thuần túy, quyết định của thuyền trưởng là hợp lý về mặt toán học. Trong nhiều tháng, các tòa án đã tranh luận về 132 mạng sống bị đánh cắp đó như một tiền lệ thường lệ trên giới hạn thiệt hại về tài sản. Hệ thống kinh tế đã học được cách chuyển sự tồn tại của con người thành các khoản ghi nợ và tín dụng, đảm bảo cái chết của chính nó thành công. Không gì có thể ngăn chặn được thương mại tam giác thông qua lời kêu gọi lòng trắc ẩn. Bởi vì tín dụng đã hàn gắn các sàn giao dịch chứng khoán châu Âu, các trạm giao dịch ở châu Phi và các đồn điền ở Caribe vào một cỗ máy tự duy trì. Và cỗ máy này không chỉ tài trợ cho các con tàu riêng lẻ. Nó bắt toàn bộ quốc gia làm con tin. Bản thân các cuộc chiến tranh đã trở thành công cụ đầu tiên và quan trọng nhất để bảo vệ các khoản đầu tư. Năm 1763, các nhà đàm phán ngồi lại ở Paris. Cuộc chiến 7 năm đã kết thúc. Pháp đã thua và theo điều kiện hòa bình phải từ bỏ một phần lãnh thổ hải ngoại. Hai món đồ đang ở trên bàn. Một bên là New France, Canada ngày nay, hàng triệu km2 rừng, hồ, và các bãi bẫy lông, có diện tích bằng một nửa diện tích châu Âu. Mặt khác, Guadaloop, một đốm núi lửa nhỏ ở Caribe mà các quan chức thuộc địa có thể cưỡi ngựa băng qua trong một ngày. Anh cho Pháp quyền lựa chọn nên giữ cái nào. và ngoại trưởng Pháp, Công tước Desoiselle, bàn giao toàn bộ lục địa phía bắc cho Nước Anh chỉ để giữ lấy hòn đảo nhỏ bé đó. Từ góc độ thuận lợi ngày nay, điều đó có vẻ giống như một trong những sai lầm lớn nhất của lịch sử. Nhưng sổ cái hải quan từ những năm 1750 lại kể một câu chuyện rất khác. Tổng lượng xuất khẩu gỗ và da hải ly hàng năm của Canada đã mang về cho ngân khố Pháp khoảng 14.000 bảng Anh một năm. Guadaloop trong cùng thời kỳ đó đã sản xuất khoảng 600.000 lb đường. Hòn đảo nhỏ đó đã sản sinh ra mọi thuộc địa duy nhất ở vùng Caribe của Anh cộng lại. Bài viết của Voltater lúc đó chế nhạo hai đế quốc đã chia cắt nhau về cái mà ông gọi là vài mẫu tuyết. Tuyết không cung cấp thức ăn cho các nhà máy và nó không trả được các khoản vay. London đã bị mắc kẹt trong phiên bản riêng của sự điên rồ này. Vương miện Anh chiến thắng đã tự nguyện trao lại giải thưởng có lợi nhất cho mình. Một khối được tổ chức chặt chẽ gồm các nghị sĩ, thương gia và chủ đồn điền, được gọi là Tây Ấn quan tâm, ngồi trong quốc hội. Họ sở hữu đất đai ở Jamaica và lo sợ sự cạnh tranh nội bộ. Nếu Anh sáp nhập Guadaloop với sản lượng khổng lồ, đường giá rẻ của Pháp sẽ có tràn ngập thị trường London. Điều đó sẽ khiến giá cả sụt giảm và xóa sạch vận may cũ chỉ sau một đêm. Thế là vận động hành lang đồn điền dựa mạnh vào nội các, cho rằng an ninh lục địa là quan trọng hơn là giành lấy lãnh thổ nhiệt đới mới. Năm 1759, hạm đội Anh tấn công Guadaloop. Người Anh nắm quyền kiểm soát các ngôi nhà sôi sục của nó và gửi các báo cáo rực rỡ về nhà tuyên bố riêng các đồn điền trên đảo có thể trang trải một nửa chi phí chiến tranh của vương miện. Bốn năm sau, các chính trị gia London đơn giản trao lại nó. Các chiến lược gia người Anh đã tự thuyết phục mình rằng việc chiếm Canada từ tay Pháp sẽ đảm bảo vĩnh viễn của họ Thuộc địa Bắc Mỹ khỏi mọi mối đe dọa phía bắc. Xếp các hồ sơ hải quan vào bản đồ các chiến dịch quân sự cho thấy một mô hình đáng lo ngại. Các đế chế không thương lượng về dặm [âm nhạc] vuông. Họ đang mặc cả về trọng tải. Các cuộc chiến trong tương lai sẽ được đo bằng thùng rượu rum. Bằng cách giữ Guadaloop và nước láng giềng Martineique, Pháp đã tiếp cận được vị trí thứ 18 phiên bản thế kỷ của dầu ngọt. Nguồn tài nguyên đó đã tài trợ cho quân đội và duy trì dòng tín dụng. Trong khi đó, nước Anh có lục địa phía bắc vô tận đòi hỏi phải có quân đồn trú, pháo đài và số lượng đáng kinh ngạc của chi tiêu cơ sở hạ tầng. Logic hoàn toàn hợp lý đó có một tác dụng phụ chết người. Khoảnh khắc mối đe dọa xâm lược của Pháp từ [âm nhạc] Canada biến mất, thực dân Mỹ không có họ còn cảm thấy cần binh lính London bảo vệ họ nữa. Khi kẻ thù bên ngoài đã biến mất, các thuộc địa đột nhiên bắt đầu hỏi tại sao họ lại trả tiền thuế cho một vương miện xa xôi chút nào. Một bài đọc lịch sử về các sự kiện cho rằng việc loại bỏ mối đe dọa từ Pháp đã đánh bại điều rất quan trọng đã giúp thực dân trung thành và giúp tạo tiền đề cho người Mỹ Cuộc cách mạng. Trong khi các thủ đô châu Âu vẽ lại đường viền [âm nhạc] trên giấy thì cỗ máy vẫn tiếp tục quay trong Caribe. Một hòn đảo đủ mạnh để lấn át một nửa Bắc Mỹ trên bàn đàm phán vẫn là một khu vực kiệt sức hoàn toàn của con người. Tỷ lệ tử vong trên các cánh đồng mía ở Guadaloop luôn ở mức 10% mỗi năm. Dân số được duy trì hoàn toàn nhờ nguồn cung cấp liên tục của người dân từ Châu Phi. Những người theo chủ nghĩa bãi nô ở Anh sau này đã viết một cách cay đắng rằng đế chế đã đánh đổi mạng sống của người da đen để lấy tuyết ở các thuộc địa và sau đó rửa sạch toàn bộ sự việc. Chính trị toàn cầu bị xiềng xích trong một dải khí hậu nhiệt đới hẹp. Kiểm soát vùng khí hậu đó đã trở thành chìa khóa cho toàn cầu hóa trong mắt các đế chế sự thống trị.
